approachQuestion.prompt: A skyline consists of n adjacent unit-width columns with nonnegative integer heights. Build exactly that solid skyline using the fewest axis-aligned rectangular blocks. Blocks may span consecutive whole columns and have positive integer heights; their interiors must be disjoint, and their union must be exactly the region from ground to each column’s height, without gaps or overhangs. Return the minimum number of blocks. Example: [2,2,1,3,1] returns 3: a height-1 block across all five columns, a height-1 block over the first two columns, and a height-2 block over column 3 (zero-based). [0,0] returns 0. Choose the best approach.
constraints: The input is immutable; n is between 1 and 200,000. All integers, indices, counts, and arithmetic results fit in signed 64-bit machine words; comparisons and arithmetic have unit cost.
Input and returned output are excluded from auxiliary space. Working stacks, arrays, and copies count. No hashing is used.

options.text: Scan heights with an increasing stack of open top levels. Pop levels above the current height. If the current height is positive and differs from the remaining top (or the stack is empty), push it and increment the block count. Otherwise continue existing blocks without incrementing.
options.feedback: A decrease closes blocks above the new level. An equal remaining level can continue across the column; a new exposed level requires another block. Future columns may extend that block but cannot remove the need to start it.

options.text: Use one block for each positive-height column.
options.feedback: It builds a valid skyline but is clearly wasteful: [2,2] needs only one block, not two; long constant skylines amplify the unnecessary blocks.

options.text: Return the number of distinct positive heights anywhere in the skyline.
options.feedback: A lower gap can separate regions at the same height. For [2,1,2], two distinct positive heights exist, but 3 blocks are necessary.

options.text: Start one block at the first positive column and one at each strict adjacent rise, doing nothing else.
options.feedback: A rise can reach a previously closed intermediate level that needs a new block. For [1,3,2], this gives 2 but 3 blocks are required: the third column cannot share the taller second column’s upper block without overhang.

feedback.reason: Recognize when an exposed height layer can continue and when a new block is unavoidable.
details: Close every open level above the current column. Zero needs no block. If a positive level is already the top after closing, extend it; otherwise start a new block and remember its top level. The total starts is the minimum block count.

A lower column closes open higher blocks. An equal surviving top extends an existing block, while a new positive height starts another. Counting changes in numerical height would confuse height differences with block count.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For open-height-layers, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let n be the column count. Keep only a height stack and scalar block count; do not materialize blocks, unit cells, or the skyline area.
constraints: Stack push, pop, and top take amortized constant time using a growable array; each entry uses a constant number of words. Count the working stack, but exclude input and final output. No recursive call stack or hash table is used.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Each positive level is pushed and popped at most once per originating column.
details: Each level is pushed at most once per column and popped at most once. This gives O(n) time independent of the numeric heights. An increasing skyline retains n levels and requires O(n) auxiliary space.
